title: Self-Healing Remediator v2 — ELI16 Overview
markdown:
# Self-Healing Remediator v2 — Plain-English Overview

> The one-paragraph version: Echo keeps hitting the same kinds of breakage — Node-version drift kills the database, the server can't grab its port after wake-from-sleep, Telegram messages fail to deliver. In the past few months, five separate "auto-fix" helpers shipped, each one solving its own little corner. They work, but they don't talk to each other. The Remediator is the conductor that finally makes them act like one system instead of five — and it adds a new piece, the SystemReviewer, that watches for failures we don't yet have a fix for and asks for help writing one.

---

## The problem in one breath

When Echo breaks, it's usually because the environment shifted underneath it (Homebrew bumped Node, the laptop slept too long, a database file got corrupted mid-write). Each of these has a fix. None of the fixes know about the others. So we get this pattern:

- The same problem comes back over and over because nothing remembers we already fixed it ten minutes ago.
- Two different healers can both decide to fix the same thing at the same time and step on each other.
- A new kind of failure shows up, nobody's written a fix for it, and the only thing that happens is "alert the user." Then the next time the same thing happens, we alert the user again. And again.

That's not self-healing. That's noisy.

## What's already in production

Here's what we already have working — these are the "five sprinklers" the spec talks about:

1. **NativeModuleHealer** — when the database library notices it was built for a different version of Node than the one running, it rebuilds itself and tries again. Just merged. Lives inside the memory subsystems.
2. **Lifeline preflight** — before the server starts, it checks for the same kind of mismatch and fixes it. If the server crash-loops, it escalates to a full rebuild.
3. **Delivery retry sentinel** — when a Telegram message fails to send, a durable queue tries again later instead of dropping it.
4. **System probes** — a framework that lets us write small, safe "is this still working?" checks for any subsystem.
5. **DB corruption recovery** — when a database file is detectably corrupt, the system quarantines it and falls back to in-memory mode so things still kind of work.

Each one of these was built in isolation. Each one learned its own lessons in isolation. None of them share a logbook, share a cooldown, or share an "are we already trying this?" check.

## What this spec proposes

A central module — the **Remediator** — that sits above the five existing healers and gives them a shared brain:

- A shared logbook (every healing attempt across every healer goes here).
- A shared lock (only one heal of the same type at a time).
- A shared cooldown (if we've tried the same heal three times in four hours, stop trying and tell the user).
- A shared dry-run mode (new healers run in "observe-only" for a week before they're allowed to actually do anything).
- A shared decision about when to alert vs. when to stay silent (silence is earned by a successful, verified heal; alerts fire for novel failures and verification failures).

Three things the spec deliberately does NOT do:

- It does NOT rewrite the existing healers. Each one stays as it is and just exposes a second entry point the Remediator can call.
- It does NOT decide on its own which problems are "worth" fixing. Every new fix needs a human-approved spec.
- It does NOT make alerts go away during the first phase. Phase 1 of the rollout is observe-only — the Remediator records what it would have done, alerts still fire as today. Only Phase 2 lets verified successes go silent.

## The new piece: SystemReviewer

Here's the interesting bit. The Remediator only knows about failures we've already taught it. So what about the ones we haven't?

The SystemReviewer is a sibling module that:

1. Watches the logbook for failures the Remediator didn't have a fix for.
2. Looks for patterns — if the same unknown failure shows up at least three times across at least two sessions over two weeks, that's not noise, that's a real new thing.
3. Asks a small, cheap LLM (Haiku-class) to write a one-paragraph summary of the pattern and suggest a name for it.
4. Sends Justin a Telegram message with a link saying "Here's a new pattern I keep seeing — want to write a fix for it?"

The SystemReviewer cannot write fixes itself. It cannot mark problems as solved. It cannot turn off alerts. It can only **suggest**, and a human has to decide whether the suggestion is real.

This gives us a bottom-up learning loop. The system grows its own playbook through human-approved expansion, not through anything trying to be clever by itself.

## The safeguards (the part Round 1 review hammered on)

The four reviewers in Round 1 surfaced 49 concerns. The 17 amendments that came out of them all do one of three things:

**Prevent the Remediator from acting as authority it doesn't have.**
- The thing the Remediator passes to a healer (a "remediation context") is now signed with a one-shot cryptographic token, microsecond-lifetime. Code that doesn't have a valid token can't pretend it's running under Remediator authority — it falls back to the old in-line behavior.
- The healers and the Remediator can both try to fix the same problem at the same time only by acquiring a shared lock first. The lock — not a recency check — is what actually prevents double-execution.
- Healers that hang have a hard deadline. The Remediator aborts them and kills child processes. The lock is force-released. The user gets alerted.

**Prevent the system from accidentally hurting itself.**
- A healer that fails verification three times in four hours across any number of restarts stops trying and falls back to alert-only. This closes the "every wake-from-sleep triggers a fresh full rebuild" loop.
- A healer marked "essential" (like the ABI-mismatch one) has a stricter quarantine threshold so a noisy false-positive can't kill self-heal entirely.
- Verification has to assert **durable** state, not just live state. A database falling back to in-memory mode is "live" but "lossy" — that emits a non-silenceable durability-degraded event so the user always knows.

**Prevent the SystemReviewer from being weaponized.**
- It cannot generate more than three open proposals at a time. The rest are silently queued.
- All proposals from one hourly tick batch into ONE message — no notification floods.
- The LLM gets a fixed safety frame at the top of every prompt, the output schema is strictly validated, and any code/URLs/imperative verbs are stripped from the summary before it's persisted or shown.
- A proposal that suggests a name colliding with an existing fix is auto-rejected.
- A proposal-derived PR can't be authored by the same agent that produced the proposal AND merged by Justin without an explicit countersigned approval. CI enforces this — not gentlemen's agreement.

## What ships when

The spec lays out a foundation-first build order. The five existing healers stay as they are. The new code lands in three waves:

- **Foundation PRs** (eight of them) — the shared logbook, the shared lock, the trust source, the supervisor handshake, the migrator primitive, the Remediator skeleton. Nothing user-visible. Has to ship first because the existing healers don't have these.
- **Wrapper PRs** (four of them) — each existing healer gets a second entry point so the Remediator can drive it. Existing in-line entry points stay — they're the safety net if the Remediator is disabled.
- **SystemReviewer PRs** (three of them) — only after the wrappers have been running long enough to produce real audit history. Earliest the SystemReviewer can ship is two weeks after the foundation hits main.

The supervisor handshake has its own special rule: it has to be on main and auto-updated to all agents for at least a week before any wrapper PR is allowed to merge. This closes the half-upgrade window where new Remediator code would talk to old server code.

## Where we are right now

- v1 spec converged April 23. Was never built.
- Five point-solutions shipped between then and now.
- v2 spec (this one) was rewritten over the last few hours to be the conductor, not a rewrite.
- Round 1 of the convergent review is done. 49 findings, 17 amendments folded in.
- Three more internal rounds + one cross-model round (GPT/Gemini/Grok) still ahead.

Nothing is approved yet. Nothing is being built yet. The convergence pattern is what decides if this is the right shape — once it's done, Justin reads the final report and either approves or not.

## What you actually need to decide

Reading-this-overview level: **does the "conductor over existing healers" framing feel right?** That's the big shape decision. Everything below it is plumbing the review process can shake out.

If yes: I keep going through rounds 2-4 and the cross-model round, then come back with the converged spec for approval.

If no: I stop and we re-shape before more review effort gets spent.
